query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3, degradation during high‐temperature exposure is governed by selective reactions of high-affinity elements (Al, Ti, and Cr) at grain boundaries. Under oxidizing conditions, these elements form a discontinuous, fragile oxide layer that initially offers passivation but later spalls due to thermal stresses, while under reducing conditions, the absence of a robust oxide scale leads to elemental depletion at grain boundaries, ultimately promoting intergranular embrittlement and catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated, single-phase fcc high-entropy alloy produced by additive manufacturing with inherent microstructural heterogeneities (e.g., grain boundary variations and residual stresses).
generation.intervention: Expose samples to controlled high-temperature conditions (600°C–900°C) in distinctly oxidizing versus reducing atmospheres and, separately, modify heat treatments to alter grain boundary element partitioning.
generation.conditions: Long-duration high-temperature exposures (e.g., ~800°C for 100 hours) under controlled oxygen partial pressures (for oxidizing conditions) or controlled reducing gas environments (e.g., with low oxygen content or added H2), at atmospheric pressure.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and the reaction layers that form there (either oxide scales or dealloyed, weakened zones).
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation (or lack thereof) at grain boundaries leads to formation of a heterogeneous, stress-prone oxide layer in oxidizing atmospheres, which spalls and compromises mechanical integrity, whereas in reducing atmospheres the minimal formation of a protective scale causes elemental depletion at grain boundaries, resulting in intergranular embrittlement and triggering catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-fabricated baseline, samples exposed to oxidizing conditions will develop a non-uniform, thin oxide scale that eventually spalls (indicating mechanical degradation), while samples under reducing conditions will show less or no protective oxide formation, leading to faster elemental depletion at grain boundaries and earlier onset of intergranular cracking and catastrophic failure.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured alloy state without prolonged high-temperature gas exposure.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected under exposures at elevated temperatures between approximately 600°C and 900°C for durations on the order of 100 hours; deviations outside these limits may lead to altered kinetics or different dominant degradation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of oxide scale formation versus elemental diffusion and the relative contributions of these processes to catastrophic failure remain uncertain due to microstructural variability inherent to additive manufacturing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the alloy and expose them at ~800°C for 100 hours in two separate atmospheres: one oxidizing (with controlled oxygen partial pressure) and one reducing (with a specified low oxygen/high H2 content). After exposure, perform detailed microstructural analyses (using SEM/TEM and EDS mapping) to examine grain boundary reaction layers and carry out mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness, hardness) to assess degradation.
measurements: Morphology and continuity of oxide or reaction layers at grain boundaries (via SEM/TEM)
Elemental distribution changes at grain boundaries (via EDS mapping)
Presence and propagation of intergranular cracks
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured microstructural and mechanical differences between the oxidizing and reducing conditions are negligible relative to the as-fabricated baseline – specifically, if no significant difference in grain boundary reaction layer formation or intergranular cleavage is observed – then the hypothesis that selective grain boundary reactions govern degradation and drive catastrophic failure is falsified.
